new.title: Walk the full length of the East Side Gallery
new.desc: The longest surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall, a good 1.3 km along Mühlenstraße, was painted by artists from around the world in spring 1990. Dmitri Vrubel's kiss between Brezhnev and Honecker and Thierry Noir's cartoon heads are the ones everyone looks for.
new.tip: Come early in the morning for photos without crowds, and walk the river side too: the back of the Wall faces the Spree.

new.title: Cross the Oberbaumbrücke on foot
new.desc: This brick Gothic double-decker from 1896 looks like a city gate, carries the yellow U-Bahn on top and was a border crossing between East and West. Today it ties Friedrichshain to Kreuzberg, with buskers under the arcades.
new.tip: Look up inside the arcade after dark for Thorsten Goldberg's neon hands playing rock, paper, scissors across the old border.

new.title: Stand beneath the Soviet soldier in Treptower Park
new.desc: The Sowjetisches Ehrenmal, opened in 1949, is both a monument and a cemetery for around 5,000 Red Army soldiers who fell in the Battle of Berlin. A 12 metre bronze soldier holding a rescued child towers over a broken swastika at the far end.
new.tip: Enter through the stone arch on Puschkinallee and walk the whole axis slowly: the scale only sinks in from the top of the mound.

new.title: Spot the Molecule Man in the Spree
new.desc: Three 30 metre aluminium figures, riddled with holes, lean into each other in the middle of the river where Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Treptow meet. American artist Jonathan Borofsky meant the holes as the molecules of all people coming together.
new.tip: The riverside path by the Treptowers gives the closest view; from the Oberbaumbrücke you get it with the whole river in front.

new.title: Stroll down Karl-Marx-Allee
new.desc: East Germany's showpiece boulevard, built in the 1950s as Stalinallee, is 90 metres wide and lined with tiled 'wedding cake' apartment palaces. Hermann Henselmann's twin towers at Frankfurter Tor and Strausberger Platz frame it at either end.
new.tip: Walk from Frankfurter Tor towards Strausberger Platz and look closely at the ceramic facades; the U5 runs underneath if your legs give up.

new.title: Climb the Kreuzberg in Viktoriapark
new.desc: The 66 metre hill that gave Kreuzberg its name is topped by Schinkel's cast-iron monument to the wars against Napoleon. In summer an artificial waterfall tumbles down the slope, and there is even a tiny city vineyard on the side.
new.tip: Go up for sunset: the view runs straight down Großbeerenstraße to the city centre. The waterfall only runs in the warm months.

new.title: Step down into the Körnerpark
new.desc: Hidden between Neukölln apartment blocks, this neo-baroque garden sits several metres below street level in a former gravel pit. Fountains, a cascade and an orangery make it feel like a small palace park that somebody misplaced.
new.tip: The orangery houses a free gallery and a café, and on summer weekends there are free concerts on its forecourt.

new.title: Find the Bohemian village in Rixdorf
new.desc: Around Richardplatz, Neukölln suddenly turns into a village: cobblestones, low houses and barns left by Protestant refugees from Bohemia who settled here in 1737. The smithy on the square was first recorded in 1624 and is still at work.
new.tip: Wander through Kirchgasse and look for the Comenius-Garten on Richardstraße. In Advent the square hosts the traditional Alt-Rixdorfer Weihnachtsmarkt, and the smithy joins in.

new.title: Meet the fairy tales at the Märchenbrunnen
new.desc: At the entrance to Volkspark Friedrichshain, Berlin's oldest public park, Ludwig Hoffmann's fountain from 1913 is crowded with 106 stone figures from German fairy tales. Behind it, two wooded hills hide wartime bunkers buried under rubble.
new.tip: After the fountain, climb the larger Bunkerberg for a leafy view, then join the locals on the lawns.

new.title: Circle the Wasserturm in Prenzlauer Berg
new.desc: Berlin's first large water tower, finished in 1877, is the round brick landmark of the Kollwitzkiez and has flats inside its thick walls. The streets around it and nearby Kollwitzplatz are the picture-book version of restored Prenzlauer Berg.
new.tip: Combine it with the weekly market on nearby Kollwitzplatz, then walk up the little hill next to the tower for a quiet bench.

new.title: See everyday East Germany at the Kulturbrauerei
new.desc: The former Schultheiss brewery, a castle-like brick complex from the 1880s, now holds cinemas, clubs and theatres. Its museum shows daily life in the GDR, from holiday campers to shortage shopping, and does not charge admission.
new.tip: Enter the courtyards from Knaackstraße or Sredzkistraße. In Advent the yards fill with the Nordic-themed Lucia Christmas market.

new.title: Hunt for street art on the RAW-Gelände
new.desc: This former railway repair yard next to Warschauer Straße is Friedrichshain at its scruffiest: crumbling halls covered in murals and paste-ups, with clubs, a skate hall, galleries and a climbing tower built onto an old bunker.
new.tip: By day it is all about the walls and the weekend flea market; after dark the same yards turn into one of the city's busiest going-out areas.

new.title: See the giant telescope at the Archenhold-Sternwarte
new.desc: The observatory in Treptower Park owns a 21 metre refractor built for the 1896 trade exhibition, called the longest movable telescope in the world. Albert Einstein gave his first public talk on general relativity here in 1915.
new.tip: The huge tube rests on the roof and can be seen from the park, but check the programme for guided tours and observation evenings.

new.title: See Berlin through its art at the Berlinische Galerie
new.desc: This museum collects only art made in Berlin since 1870: Dada, New Objectivity, photography and architecture models. It is housed in a 1960s warehouse where West Berlin once stored emergency window glass.
new.tip: It sits in a quiet residential corner of Kreuzberg, an easy walk from the Jewish Museum, so the two combine well on a grey day.

new.title: Watch the evening from the Admiralbrücke
new.desc: On mild evenings this wrought-iron bridge from 1882 over the Landwehrkanal turns into Kreuzberg's open-air living room. People sit on the cobbles with a drink, musicians play and the canal goes golden.
new.tip: Bring your own drink from a Späti (late-night corner shop) and be considerate: neighbours live right here and the bridge is cleared at 10 pm.

new.title: Walk to the Eierhäuschen and the lost Spreepark
new.desc: Deep in the Plänterwald, East Germany's only permanent amusement park has been asleep since 2002 and is slowly being turned into an art and nature park. The restored riverside excursion house Eierhäuschen next door has been open again since 2024 with exhibitions and a beer garden.
new.tip: Follow the Spree path from Treptower Park past the Insel der Jugend. The park itself is still fenced off, so look out for the guided tours.

new.title: Eat your way through Street Food Thursday at Markthalle Neun
new.desc: A 19th-century market hall in the middle of Kreuzberg, saved by locals and now the city's best-known food hall. On Thursday evenings the weekly market makes way for street food stalls from all over the world.
new.tip: Go with friends and share, so you can try more stalls. Fridays and Saturdays are for the big produce market; the hall is closed on Sundays.

new.title: Snack along the Turkish market on the Maybachufer
new.desc: Twice a week the canal bank fills with stalls piled with vegetables, olives, cheese, flatbread and rolls of fabric, and sellers shouting their last offers. It is the loudest, tastiest slice of Kreuzkölln life.
new.tip: It runs on Tuesdays and Fridays. Pick up gözleme or dips and eat them on the canal wall; prices drop towards closing time.

new.title: Queue for Mustafa's Gemüse Kebap
new.desc: Berlin's most famous kebab is a chicken döner stuffed with fried vegetables, feta and a squeeze of lemon. In 2025 the legendary street stall on Mehringdamm moved into a proper shop across the road, and the queue simply followed.
new.tip: The line builds from late morning and can easily take half an hour. Watch out for copycats with similar names and check you are at the Mehringdamm shop.

new.title: Have a Currywurst standing up at Curry 36
new.desc: A few steps from Mustafa's, this Mehringdamm stand is the West Berlin answer to the Currywurst question. You eat at high tables on the pavement, shoulder to shoulder with taxi drivers and night owls.
new.tip: Order it 'ohne Darm' (without skin) for the classic Berlin style, with chips and mayonnaise on the side.

new.title: Try the East Berlin Currywurst at Konnopke's Imbiß
new.desc: Max Konnopke started selling sausages on this corner in 1930, and his family is credited with bringing Currywurst to East Berlin in 1960. The kiosk still stands under the rattling U2 viaduct at Eberswalder Straße.
new.tip: It keeps limited daytime hours, so do not plan it as a midnight snack; eat at the standing tables while the trains rattle overhead.

new.title: Eat a burger in a former public toilet
new.desc: The original Burgermeister grills in a listed old public toilet under the elevated U-Bahn at Schlesisches Tor. It opened in 2006 after years of fighting for a permit and has been a Kreuzberg late-night ritual ever since.
new.tip: Trains rumble overhead while you eat at the standing tables. The chilli burger is seriously hot, you have been warned.

new.title: Drink a beer under the chestnuts at Prater
new.desc: Beer has been poured on this spot off Kastanienallee since 1837, which makes Prater the oldest beer garden in Berlin. Hundreds of seats on long benches under old trees, with a Bratwurst and pretzel hatch.
new.tip: The garden opens in fair weather during the warm months; it is self-service, so grab a table first and send one person to the counter.

new.title: Find the rooftop bar on a Neukölln car park
new.desc: Klunkerkranich is a ramshackle garden bar on the top deck of the Neukölln Arcaden shopping centre, with wooden huts, DJs, concerts and a wide view over the rooftops towards the TV tower.
new.tip: Use the entrance by the library and post office on Karl-Marx-Straße, take the lift to parking level 5 and walk up the ramp. Sunset is the busy hour.

new.title: Taste a classic Döner at Imren Grill in Neukölln
new.desc: While visitors queue elsewhere, plenty of Berliners swear by Imren on Karl-Marx-Straße for the traditional kind: juicy, well seasoned meat, fresh salad and homemade sauces in crisp bread. It regularly lands near the top of best Döner rankings.
new.tip: The branch by Rathaus Neukölln is the one critics single out. Look beyond the Döner too: lahmacun, pide and gözleme are all made here.

new.title: Brunch in a cemetery chapel at 21 Gramm
new.desc: This café has moved into a former mortuary chapel on the St. Thomas churchyard off Hermannstraße. High vaulted ceilings, arched windows and a garden terrace between old trees make it Neukölln's most unusual breakfast spot.
new.tip: It is a daytime café and popular at weekends, so come early or be ready to wait for a table.

new.title: Have a riverside drink at Holzmarkt 25
new.desc: The makers of the legendary Bar 25 turned this stretch of former border strip on the Spree into a cooperative wooden village with a bar, bakery, restaurants and a concert hall. It still feels wonderfully improvised.
new.tip: Head for the Marktplatz bar and take your drink down to the water's edge. In late autumn the site hosts its own winter market.

new.title: Sit by the Spree at Zenner
new.desc: Excursion-goers have been stopping at this spot in Treptower Park since the 1820s. The big riverside house, right opposite the Insel der Jugend, has been revived with a beer garden, a wine garden, an ice cream parlour and concerts.
new.tip: Make it the reward at the end of a walk along the river from S-Bahn Treptower Park, or arrive by excursion boat at Treptower Hafen.

new.title: Dig through the Mauerpark flea market
new.desc: Every Sunday the former death strip between Prenzlauer Berg and Wedding becomes Berlin's biggest flea market party: vinyl, vintage clothes, GDR relics, old bikes and a lot of food stalls. A long stretch of the Wall on the hill is a legal graffiti canvas.
new.tip: Come before noon if you actually want to browse; by the afternoon it is shoulder to shoulder. Haggling is expected.

new.title: Sing at the Bearpit Karaoke in Mauerpark
new.desc: Since 2009 a mobile sound system has rolled into the stone amphitheatre on Sunday afternoons, and anyone brave enough sings in front of a cheering crowd of hundreds. Bad singers get the loudest applause.
new.tip: It only happens in the warm season and in dry weather, starting mid-afternoon. Arrive early for a seat on the steps, or put your name down.

new.title: Ride down a runway on Tempelhofer Feld
new.desc: When Tempelhof airport closed, Berlin simply opened the gates: since 2010 the runways and meadows have been one enormous park, protected from building by a 2014 referendum. People skate, cycle, fly kites and grow vegetables where planes once landed.
new.tip: Enter from Oderstraße on the Neukölln side for the community gardens. Bring wheels and a jacket, as it is always windy, and note the gates close at dusk.

new.title: Swim in the Spree at the Badeschiff
new.desc: An old cargo barge was turned into a bright blue pool in 2004 and moored in the river at the Arena in Treptow. You swim lengths with the Oberbaumbrücke and the TV tower in view, then dry off on the sandy deck.
new.tip: It is an open-air summer pool and takes a winter break. On hot days it fills up fast, so check the website for tickets before you go.

new.title: Swim like a Roman in the Stadtbad Neukölln
new.desc: Opened in 1914 and modelled on ancient thermal baths, this public pool has columns, mosaics and two halls that look more like a temple than a swimming bath. It is an ordinary municipal pool, so anyone can do lengths here.
new.tip: The sauna area was renovated and reopened in 2026. Public swimming times differ per hall, so check the Berliner Bäder timetable first.

new.title: Follow the Landwehrkanal from Kreuzberg to Neukölln
new.desc: The canal is the green thread of the neighbourhood: lawns at Fraenkelufer, boules players and market days on the Maybachufer, cafés along Paul-Lincke-Ufer and swans in between. It is where locals spend the first warm evening of the year.
new.tip: Start at the Admiralbrücke and walk east along the water; beyond Forster Straße it gets much quieter and greener.

new.title: Browse the Sunday flea market on Boxhagener Platz
new.desc: The 'Boxi' is Friedrichshain's village square, and on Sundays its edges fill with stalls selling books, furniture, records, clothes and household oddities. It is smaller and more local than Mauerpark.
new.tip: Do it the Friedrichshain way: late brunch in one of the cafés around the square first, flea market second, lawn in the middle third.

new.title: Treasure hunt at the Nowkoelln Flowmarkt
new.desc: Every second Sunday in the season, Neuköllners empty their wardrobes and shelves along the canal: private second-hand stalls mixed with local designers, music and street food. It is the neighbourhood's favourite flea market.
new.tip: It is not weekly, so check the dates on the market's website before you go. There is also a special Advent edition.

new.title: Try your luck at the Berghain door
new.desc: The world's most talked-about techno club fills a 1950s power station behind Ostbahnhof. The door policy is famously strict and unexplained, photos are banned inside and weekend parties run from Saturday night into Monday.
new.tip: No trick is guaranteed: keep your group small, stay calm in the queue and accept a no with a shrug. Your phone camera gets a sticker at the door.

new.title: Row around the Insel der Jugend
new.desc: A small wooded island in the Spree, reached from Treptower Park by the arched Abteibrücke with its two little towers. At the foot of the bridge you can hire rowing and pedal boats and paddle out among the excursion steamers.
new.tip: Boat hire is a warm-season affair. Afterwards, the island garden is a nice place for a drink right at the water.

new.title: Play your way through the Computerspielemuseum
new.desc: On Karl-Marx-Allee, this museum tells the story of video games from Pong onwards, with a 1980s arcade hall, a giant controller and the notorious PainStation, which punishes losers for real.
new.tip: It is hands-on, so allow a couple of hours, and it is a strong rainy-day option with children or nostalgic adults.

new.title: Lean back under the dome of the Zeiss-Großplanetarium
new.desc: Opened in 1987 for the city's 750th birthday, this silver dome in Prenzlauer Berg was one of the last big buildings of the GDR. Today it shows full-dome star shows, music programmes and films under a 23 metre dome.
new.tip: Shows are in German unless marked otherwise, so check the programme for English-friendly ones. The hands-on exhibition in the foyer is free.
